summary: This unit teaches you to plan a complete work activity in a fabrication shop, from reading the work order to handing over the finished job. You will learn to find and confirm the information, break the job into steps, work out materials, costs and time, assess the risks, and plan the tools, people and work area. You will also learn to check progress and quality, deal with changes, clean up, report and review the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches you to **plan** a job before you start it, and then to follow, check and finish it as planned. A good plan saves steel, time and money, and it stops accidents, because the hazards are thought about before the sparks fly.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. The examples are everyday fabrication jobs: frames, stands, gates, grills, shelving and handrails, made in the workshop or fitted on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Read the work order, drawing and specification; take or check site measurements; ask about anything missing or unclear.
List the tasks in a sensible order, see which depend on others, and mark the hold points where work stops for a check.
Make a cut list and materials list, work out stock lengths with little waste, and estimate the cost in J$.
Estimate how long each task takes, draw a simple bar chart and check that the deadline can be met.
Identify the hazards, judge the risks and choose controls using the hierarchy of controls; arrange permits.
Plan tools, people and the work area
List and check the tools, machines and PPE, book shared equipment, set out the area and decide who does what.
Have the plan approved by the supervisor and explain it to the team in a toolbox talk.
Track progress and quality, keep records, and deal with delays, breakdowns and changes.
Inspect the job, clean up, sort the waste, hand in the records, report and learn from the job.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on understanding the task, finding information, sequence, materials and estimating, time, hazards and risk, tools, people, communication, change, progress, waste and finishing.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as JSA, SDS, SWL and deadline, and simple sums) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: writing a full work plan for a customer's fabrication job and presenting it, and planning and making a small welded frame, then reviewing the job against the plan.

blocks.note: Planning questions often include simple sums: millimetres to metres, lengths and stock lengths, costs, hours and finishing times. Work every sum twice and write the unit with every answer.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every plan starts with knowing exactly what the customer wants. Read everything before you plan anything.

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: What is to be made or repaired, how many, for whom, where, and the date it is due. It often carries a job number to put on every record.
The shape, sizes, tolerances, material, joints and weld sizes, and how the parts fit together. Check its **revision** letter or number so you use the latest one.
The standard the work must meet: steel grade, welding process and consumables, finish (for example primer and two coats of paint) and inspection.
Welding procedure (WPS), where one is used
How each weld is to be made: process, consumable, settings and joint preparation.
How to use and care for machines and fittings safely, such as a new grinder, hinges, locks or anchors.
The hazards, PPE, storage and first aid for paints, thinners, solvents and other chemicals on the job.
The real sizes where the job must fit, such as a window opening or a wall.

flow: Read the work order and drawing all the way through
Check the drawing number and revision, and that the work order and drawing are for the same job
Note what you will need: sizes, material, quantity, finish, due date
Where the job must fit on site, measure it yourself or check that the drawing's sizes were measured on site
Write down anything missing, unclear or contradictory
Ask the supervisor (or, through the supervisor, the customer or designer)
Record the answers on the job card, with the date and who said it

ul: Never guess a size, a quantity, a weld size or a material. A guess that is wrong wastes steel and time, and can make the job unsafe.
If two documents disagree, do not pick the one you like: stop and ask.
Walls, floors and openings are rarely exactly square or exactly as drawn. Measure every opening the job must fit, and measure the diagonals too.

blocks.note: Customers often send sizes as a phone photo of a sketch or a voice note. Treat these as a start, not as the final word: confirm every size in writing, or measure it yourself, before any steel is cut.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A big job is easier to plan, time, check and share when it is broken into **tasks** in a sensible order. Each task can then be given a time, a person, the tools it needs and its checks.

blocks.h: A typical order of work for a welded frame

flow: Read the drawing; make the cut list; collect and check materials
Mark out
Cut and deburr
Clean the joint areas to bright metal
Fit up and tack; check sizes, squareness and diagonals
Weld, in an order that controls distortion
Clean and grind the welds; check for faults
Final inspection against the drawing
Prime and paint; let each coat dry
Deliver and install; hand over

ul: Painting comes **after** welding and grinding. Welding burns paint off, gives off harmful fumes from it, and spoils the weld with porosity.
Checks come **before** the next step makes a fault hard to fix: check square before welding, and inspect before painting hides the welds.
Some tasks can run at the same time if there are enough people and machines: one person can cut the next set of parts while another welds.

blocks.p: A **dependency** is a link between tasks: one cannot start until another is finished. The frame must be welded before the hinges are fitted; the primer must be dry before the top coat goes on.

A **hold point** is a stage written into the plan where work must stop until a check is made and signed off, for example by the supervisor or an inspector. Typical hold points are after fit-up and tacking, and after welding, before painting.

blocks.h: Method statements and job safety analyses

head: Document
What it is
rows: A step-by-step description of how the job will be done safely: the sequence, equipment, people, hazards, controls and checks. Often needed for site work.
A form that lists each step of the job, the hazards of that step, and the controls. It is a simple risk assessment done task by task.

blocks.p: Targets in a plan should be **SMART**: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. "Work faster on the gates" is not SMART. "Fit, tack and check both gate frames to drawing G-3 by 12 noon on Wednesday" is.

When several jobs are waiting, plan the **most urgent and important** first: the one with the nearest deadline that matters most, or the one others are waiting for. Doing the easy or favourite job first is not planning.

sections.title: Materials: cut lists, quantities and cost

ul: Fabrication drawings give sizes in **millimetres (mm)**. Steel is sold in **metres (m)**, often in **6 m lengths**.
1 m = 1000 mm. To change mm to m, divide by 1000 (2450 mm = 2.45 m). To change m to mm, multiply by 1000 (1.8 m = 1800 mm).
The **perimeter** (the distance all the way round) of a rectangle is 2 × (length + width). A frame 1500 mm × 600 mm needs 2 × (1500 + 600) = 4200 mm of bar to go round it once.
Section sizes are written in a set order: flat bar 50 × 6 is 50 mm wide and 6 mm thick; SHS 40 × 40 × 3 is square hollow section 40 mm by 40 mm with a 3 mm wall.

blocks.p: A **cut list** lists every piece to be cut, with its mark, section, length and number. It comes from the drawing. Here is the cut list for a workbench frame, 1500 mm long and 600 mm deep, in 40 × 40 × 3 SHS.

head: Mark
Part
Section
Length (mm)
Number
Total (mm)
rows: Short rail (fits between the long rails: 600 − 40 − 40)

blocks.p: Read the drawing carefully at the corners: whether parts are **butted** or **mitred** changes their cut length. Here the short rails fit between the long rails, so 40 mm is taken off at each end.

A saw blade or cutting disc turns a strip of steel into dust and sparks. This strip is the **kerf**, often about 1 to 3 mm, and more for gas cutting. Allow for one kerf at every cut, plus a little to square a rough or rusty end.

blocks.note: The total above is 11.48 m, so two 6 m lengths (12 m) look enough. But four 1500 mm rails from one length need 6000 mm of steel plus three or four saw cuts: they do **not** fit. That is why you plan which pieces come from each length.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Stock length
Pieces cut from it
Steel used, with 3 mm per cut
Offcut
rows: About 369 mm: keep, marked with its size

ul: Cut the **longest pieces first**, then fill the rest of each length with shorter pieces.
Check the store for **useful offcuts** before ordering: a short piece may come from an offcut.
Measure twice and cut once: a mis-cut piece usually means another stock length.
Mark kept offcuts with their size and section and put them on the offcut rack.

blocks.h: The materials list and cost estimate

blocks.p: The **materials list** (or bill of materials) lists everything to be bought or drawn from stores, not only the steel: electrodes or wire, gas, grinding and cutting discs, primer, paint, thinners, fixings, hinges and locks. Check the **type, size, grade and quantity** of each item.

blocks.note: These prices are examples only: use the current supplier price list. You pay for **whole stock lengths**, not just the metres you use. If the prices do not include GCT, add it at the current rate, and check whether labour and delivery are to be added.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Steel is heavy. A square metre of steel plate **1 mm thick weighs about 7.85 kg**. So a 1.2 m × 2.4 m sheet of 3 mm plate weighs about 1.2 × 2.4 × 3 × 7.85 ≈ 68 kg: a job for two people or a sheet trolley, not one. A 6 m length of 40 × 40 × 3 SHS weighs about 20 kg.
Estimating time lets you plan the order of work, share it out, and see whether the **deadline** (the date or time the job must be finished) can be met.

ul: List the tasks in order and estimate each one from past jobs, from experienced workers or the supervisor, and from the number of people and machines available.
Include set-up and clean-up, checks at the hold points, and **waiting time** such as paint drying overnight.
Allow a little extra time for things that go wrong (a **contingency**). Do not plan every minute of every day.
**Person-hours** (or trainee-hours) = hours per item × number of items, or the total of every person's hours. Three people working 4 hours each is 12 person-hours.
Two people do not always halve the time: with one welding machine, only one person can weld at a time.
Time units: 1 hour = 60 minutes. 1.5 hours = 90 minutes; 45 minutes = 0.75 hours. Convert everything to the same unit before adding.

blocks.p: A working day in the plan must leave out breaks. For example, a day from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. with a 30-minute lunch gives 8 hours of work. A task of 3 hours that starts at 10:30 a.m. and runs through the 12:00–12:30 lunch finishes at 2:00 p.m.

A **bar chart**, also called a **Gantt chart**, lists the tasks down the left and the days or hours along the top. Each task is a bar from its planned start to its finish, so you can see the order, the overlaps and the finish date at a glance. Here is a plan for the workbench frame, worked by two people.

ul: During the job, mark the **actual** progress on the chart beside the planned bars. A gap shows at once that a task is late.
If the chart shows the finish after the deadline, re-plan now (more people, overtime, a different order) and tell the supervisor; do not wait until the last day.

blocks.note: Paint dries more slowly in humid, rainy weather and must not go on wet steel. In the rainy seasons, plan painting under cover and allow extra drying time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: Sparks, arc light, fumes, a live cable, a heavy beam, a tin of thinners
How likely the harm is, and how bad it could be
Sparks near dry cardboard: a fire is likely and could be serious, so the risk is high
What is done to remove the hazard or reduce the risk
Clearing the cardboard, screens, an extinguisher and a fire watch

flow: List the steps of the task
For each step, identify the hazards
Decide who could be harmed and how: you, the team, customers, the public
Judge the risk: how likely, and how serious
Choose controls, starting at the top of the hierarchy
Write it down and explain it to the team
Review it if the job, the place or the people change

blocks.p: The risk assessment is done **before** the work starts, as part of the plan, and checked again on the day. A simple way to judge the risk is to rate the likelihood and the severity as low, medium or high: a likely event with serious harm is a high risk that must be controlled before work begins.

Controls are chosen from the top down. The higher a control is, the better it works, because it depends less on people remembering to do the right thing. **PPE comes last**: it is needed, but only after the other controls.

head: Level
What it means
Fabrication examples
rows: Buy steel cut to size, so there is less cutting and grinding; take a part back to the workshop instead of welding it in a building full of people
Replace it with something less hazardous
A water-based paint instead of a solvent paint; a quieter cutting method
Physical changes that keep people away from the hazard
Welding screens, fume extraction, guards on grinders, a jig instead of holding parts by hand
Rules, permits, training, signs and planning
A hot work permit, a fire watch, keeping others out, job rotation, a toolbox talk
Helmet, gloves, safety glasses, face shield, ear protection, respirator, boots

blocks.h: Hazards to list for welding and grinding jobs

ul: Arc light and UV; fumes and gases; sparks, spatter and fire; hot metal and burns; electric shock.
Flying particles from grinding and chipping; noise; vibration.
Heavy lifting and dropped steel; sharp edges; trips over cables and offcuts.
Gas cylinders; paints, thinners and solvents (check the SDS); working at height or on site near the public.

blocks.h: Hot work permits and fire watch

blocks.p: Outside a welding bay, for example in a store room, a hotel or a factory, hot work usually needs a **hot work permit** from the person in charge of the premises. The permit lists the checks: combustibles cleared or covered, extinguishers ready, gaps and openings covered, and a **fire watch** during and after the work for the time stated (often 30 to 60 minutes). The permit is for a set place and time only.

head: Sign
Shape and colour
Meaning
Example
rows: Red circle with a diagonal bar
Blue circle with a white symbol
Wear eye protection; wear ear protection
Yellow triangle with a black border
Fire extinguisher; fire alarm call point

sections.title: Tools, equipment, people and the work area

ul: From the list of steps, write down every tool, machine, consumable and item of PPE each task needs.

Check **while planning**, not on the day, that each is available and working, so faults can be fixed or replacements found in time. Book shared machines and bays (a cut-off saw, a welding booth, the drill press) for the times in your bar chart.
Before starting, check condition: leads, plugs and inspection tags; guards; discs and blades; welding cables and clamps; measuring tools.
List the PPE for each task, so the right items are ready and in good condition for everyone.

blocks.note: A machine found faulty is not used. Isolate it, tag it DO NOT USE, report it, and change the plan around it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Decide who does each task, and check that they have the skills and training. A trainee works under supervision.
Plan **enough people or lifting equipment** for heavy or awkward items, and a safe method. Never plan for one person to lift something too heavy for one.
Lifting equipment is marked with its **safe working load (SWL)**: the most it may lift or carry. Never exceed it, and check the equipment's inspection tag.
Plan for others who may be affected: other trainees, customers, the public, children.
Arrange the area so materials flow in order: store, marking out, cutting, fitting, welding, finishing.
Keep walkways and exits clear, with no trailing cables and no materials piled in them.
Screens round welding; nothing that can burn nearby; extraction or good ventilation.
Fire extinguisher, first-aid box and the emergency switch in place, working and easy to reach.
Tools and materials for the task set out ready, the rest put away.

blocks.p: Show the plan to the supervisor **before** work starts. The supervisor can spot mistakes and missing steps, check that it fits other work in the shop, approve the cost and materials, and arrange permits. Then share the plan with the team so everyone works from the same information.
A **toolbox talk** is a short meeting at the start of the job or the day. It covers:

ul: What is being made, with the drawing, the steps and who does what.
The deadline and the hold points.
The main hazards and controls from the risk assessment, and the PPE to wear.
Where the extinguisher and first-aid box are, and what to do in an emergency.
Who to report problems to; then questions.

sections.title: Carrying out the plan: progress, quality and change

ul: Compare the work done with the plan at set times, for example at the end of each session, and mark the bar chart.
When a task runs late, find out why and tell the supervisor early, so there is time to put it right.
Never catch up by skipping quality checks, rushing safety steps or leaving off PPE.

head: Stage
Check
rows: Lengths and angles against the cut list; ends square; burrs removed
Sizes, squareness, diagonals, gaps; parts in the right place and the right way round
Weld sizes, faults (porosity, undercut, cracks), distortion; sizes still correct
Final inspection against the drawing and specification; surface clean
Coverage and finish; fixings tight; job level, plumb and working

blocks.p: Keep records on the job card, time sheet or inspection sheet: tasks done and when, time taken, materials used, results of each check, faults and what was done about them, with names and dates. Records show the work was done properly and are used at the review.
A **contingency plan** says in advance what you will do if something goes wrong: a second supplier, a spare machine, other tasks that can be done while waiting. When a problem happens:

flow: Make the situation safe (stop, switch off and isolate a faulty machine, tag it)
Tell the supervisor straight away what happened and how it affects the plan
Choose an option: other tasks first, another machine or supplier, a different order of work
If the deadline will be missed, the supervisor tells the customer early and agrees a new date
Update the plan and the bar chart and tell the team
Record what happened, for the review

head: Problem
Sensible options
rows: Do tasks that do not need them first (jigs, other parts, paint area); another supplier; re-plan
Tag it out and report it; use another machine; change the order of work
Share the tasks out again; check the skills needed; adjust the dates
Do workshop tasks first; plan site work and painting for dry days
Record it; the supervisor agrees the extra cost and time with the customer in writing; update the drawing, cut list and plan before the work changes

blocks.note: Never make a change quietly because a customer asked for it on site. A change that is not recorded and approved can leave the job wrong on the drawing, unpaid for, or unsafe.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Finishing: clean-up, waste, reporting and review

blocks.p: A work activity is **complete** only when the job is inspected and accepted, the area is cleaned up, the tools are returned and the records are handed in, not as soon as the last weld is made.

flow: Final inspection against the drawing and specification; results recorded
Machines switched off and isolated; gas cylinder valves closed
Tools cleaned, checked and returned; damage reported
Useful offcuts marked with their size and put on the rack; scrap metal in the scrap bin
Electrode stubs in the metal stub bin; used discs, empty tins and rags in the right bins (rags with solvent in a closed metal bin)
Floor swept and walkways cleared

ul: Plan the cuts so each stock length is used with little waste, and reuse offcuts on later jobs.
Scrap steel is collected for recycling: keep it apart from general rubbish.
Never burn waste, pour paint or thinners down a drain, or dump rubbish in gullies or bush.

blocks.p: Hand the supervisor the completed job card, inspection records, materials used and time taken, with a report of any problems, faults, near misses or changes. The finished item is handed to the customer or the store, with any care instructions.
A **review** after the job is how a team gets better. It is about learning, not blaming. Compare the actual with the plan:

head: Question
Example
rows: Time: did each task take as long as planned?
Welding took 3 hours, not 2: the welder had to stop for a booth booked by another group
Materials: did we use what we planned?
One extra length was needed because a rail was cut 50 mm short
Quality: did the checks catch faults in time?
The frame was out of square after welding; the welding order needs changing
Sparks reached the store door: move the grinding bench next time
Book the booth for the whole afternoon; one person checks every cut against the cut list

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can read a work order, drawing and specification and say what the job needs.
I can find information in manuals and safety data sheets and confirm anything unclear with the supervisor.
I can break a job into steps in a sensible order and show the dependencies and hold points.
I can write SMART targets and put urgent, important jobs first.
I can make a cut list, plan the cuts from stock lengths, allow for the kerf and keep waste low.
I can make a materials list and estimate the cost in J$.
I can estimate times, work out person-hours and finishing times, and draw a bar chart.
I can explain hazard and risk, carry out a simple risk assessment and use the hierarchy of controls.
I can say when a hot work permit and a fire watch are needed and read safety signs.
I can plan the tools, equipment, PPE, people and work area, and check them before the job.
I can explain the plan to the team in a toolbox talk.
I can check progress and quality during a job and keep records.
I can deal with delays, breakdowns and customer changes.
I can finish a job: inspect, clean up, sort waste, hand in records, report and review.

terms: A chart showing each task as a bar from its start to its finish
A list of all the materials needed, with sizes and quantities
A plan for what to do if something goes wrong
Something done to remove a hazard or reduce a risk
A list of every piece to cut, with its section, length and number
The date or time by which a job must be finished
A link between tasks: one cannot start until another is finished
A person checking for fire during and after hot work
Eliminate, substitute, engineering controls, administrative controls, PPE: best first
A stage where work stops until a check is made and signed off
Written permission, with checks, to weld, cut or grind in a place that is not a welding bay
Job safety analysis: each step of a job with its hazards and controls
The width of metal removed by a saw blade or cutting disc
A step-by-step plan of how a job will be done safely
The total of every person's working hours on a job
How likely harm is, and how bad it could be
Safety data sheet: the safety facts about a product
The length steel is sold in, often 6 m

A short safety and planning briefing at the start of a job or day
The instruction saying what job is to be done, how many, for whom and by when

c1.title: Store-room shelving for a pharmacy in Falmouth
c1.text: Kerry-Ann, a Level 2 trainee, is given a work order by her supervisor, Ms Henry: make and fit three steel shelving units in the store room of a pharmacy in Falmouth, Trelawny, to drawing SH-02, within 14 days. The drawing shows the units 2100 mm tall. When Kerry-Ann visits the store room, she finds a concrete beam across the ceiling only 2000 mm above the floor. The units are to be bolted to a block wall, and the pharmacy stays open to customers during the work.

c2.title: Trestle stands for a hardware store in Bog Walk
c2.text: Nadine is planning materials for two trestle stands for a hardware store in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The cut list needs 8 legs, each 700 mm long, and 4 top bars, each 900 mm long, all in 40 × 40 × 3 SHS. The supplier sells this tube only in 6 m lengths, at J$ 8 900 per length. Each saw cut removes about 3 mm.

c3.title: A carport frame in Old Harbour
c3.text: Rohan, a welder, and Tamika, a trainee, are building a steel carport frame for a house in Old Harbour, St Catherine. Their bar chart lists: A mark and cut, B clean and deburr, C fit and tack, D weld, E grind and clean, F inspection by the supervisor, G prime, H top coat, I install on site, and J cut and drill six base plates from the cut list. The shop has one welding machine. The plan leaves one night between G and H.

c4.title: Repairing a rack in a Negril hotel laundry
c4.text: Garfield, a welder, and Alicia, a trainee, must repair a cracked steel rack in a hotel laundry in Negril, Westmoreland. The rack can be unbolted from the wall. The laundry is busy, with staff passing, lint (fluff) from the dryers on the floor and ledges, and bottles of bleach and a solvent stain remover on a shelf nearby. The hotel's maintenance manager issues hot work permits for any welding on the premises.

c5.title: A tuck-shop door in Annotto Bay
c5.text: Mr Thompson's team is making a steel security door for a school tuck shop in Annotto Bay, St Mary. Their plan allowed 20 hours of work. On day 2 the cut-off saw stops, with a smell of burning. On day 3 the principal asks for a small serving hatch to be added to the door. The job is finished after 26 hours, and one extra length of tube was used because a rail was cut short.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do about the beam before going further with the plan?
o: Make the units 2100 mm as drawn, since the drawing is the instruction
Cut the units down to fit on the day they are fitted in the store room
Record the beam height and raise it with Ms Henry before going on
Make the units shorter herself and say nothing, as it is a small change
questions.why: The site does not match the drawing. Guessing either way risks a wasted job, so she records the real measurement and gets a decision, through the supervisor, before materials are cut.

questions.q: Which document tells Kerry-Ann how many units to make, for whom and by when?
o: The work order
The safety data sheet
The drawing's parts list
The supplier's price list
questions.why: The work order (job card) gives what is to be done, the quantity, the customer and the due date. The drawing gives the shape and sizes.

questions.q: The units will be bolted to the pharmacy's block wall. Which item must her tools list include that a workshop-only job would not?
o: A tape measure and a steel rule for checking sizes
A hammer drill, masonry bits and a cable detector
Welding helmets and leather gloves for everyone
A file and a file card for cleaning up the cut ends
questions.why: Fixing to a block wall needs holes drilled in masonry, and a check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling. Planning site tools in advance avoids a wasted trip back to the workshop.

questions.q: The pharmacy stays open during the fitting. What should the plan include?
o: Fitting the units as fast as possible so customers are not delayed
Asking customers to wear safety glasses while they are in the shop
Leaving all the tools out overnight so that the work starts sooner next day
A time agreed with the pharmacy and the work area kept clear of customers
questions.why: Members of the public can be harmed by drilling, falling parts and trailing cables. The plan agrees a suitable time with the customer and keeps the work area closed off.

questions.q: What total length of tube do the pieces need, ignoring saw cuts?
questions.why: Legs: 8 × 700 mm = 5600 mm. Top bars: 4 × 900 mm = 3600 mm. Total 9200 mm = 9.2 m.

questions.q: With a cutting plan, how many 6 m lengths must Nadine order?
o: 2 lengths
1 length
3 lengths
4 lengths
questions.why: One length gives all 8 legs (5600 mm plus 8 cuts of 3 mm = 5624 mm). A second gives the 4 top bars (3600 + 12 = 3612 mm), leaving a long offcut to keep.

questions.q: What should Nadine put in the estimate for the cost of the tube?
o: About J$ 13 650
questions.why: Tube is bought in whole 6 m lengths: 2 × J$ 8 900 = J$ 17 800. About J$ 13 650 is the cost of 9.2 m at the metre rate, but the supplier does not sell part lengths.

questions.q: Before ordering, the store finds four offcuts of the same tube, each 1.0 m long and in good condition. How many new lengths are now needed?
o: None
3 lengths
2 lengths
1 length
questions.why: Each 1.0 m offcut gives one 900 mm top bar, so all four bars come from stock. Only the legs need new tube, and one 6 m length holds all eight. Always check stock and offcuts before ordering.

questions.q: Why does the plan leave a night between priming (G) and the top coat (H)?
o: The primer must dry before the top coat goes on
Welders are not allowed to paint on the same day
The top coat is cheaper if it is bought the next day
The frame must cool down from welding overnight
questions.why: Paint put on wet primer can wrinkle, peel or trap solvent. Drying time is a real part of the schedule, and in humid weather it may take longer.

questions.q: Task F is a hold point. What does this mean for Rohan and Tamika?
o: They may skip F if the job is running behind
They hold the frame in clamps until the welds cool
F can be done at any time after the frame is installed
Work stops until the supervisor has checked the frame
questions.why: At a hold point work must not go past that stage until the check is made and signed off. Inspecting before priming means faults are found while they can still be seen and fixed.

questions.q: With only one welding machine, which task can Tamika usefully do while Rohan welds (D)?
o: E, grinding and cleaning all the welds on the frame
G, priming the parts of the frame already welded
J, cutting and drilling the base plates
I, installing the frame on site in Old Harbour
questions.why: J needs only the cut list, not the welded frame, so it can run at the same time as D. E, G and I all depend on the welding being finished and inspected.

questions.q: Which control is highest in the hierarchy of controls for this repair?
o: Unbolt the rack and repair it in the workshop
Put up welding screens all around the rack area
Give the laundry staff ear plugs and goggles
Put a warning sign on the laundry door
questions.why: Taking the rack to the workshop removes the hot work hazard from the laundry altogether, which is elimination. Screens are engineering controls, signs are administrative, and PPE comes last.

questions.q: Why does Alicia list the lint on the risk assessment as a hazard?
o: It burns very easily if sparks land in it
It makes the floor slippery for the welder
It blocks the welding machine's air vents
It stains the weld and makes it weaker
questions.why: Fine, dry fluff catches fire easily from sparks and spatter, and can smoulder unseen. It must be cleared or covered before any hot work.

questions.q: If the welding is done in the laundry, who should the hot work permit come from?
o: Garfield, as he is the welder who is doing the work
The hotel's maintenance manager, before work starts
Any laundry worker who happens to be on duty at the time
No one, if the job takes less than an hour
questions.why: The permit is issued by the person responsible for the premises, who knows the building's hazards. It sets the checks, the place and the time, and is in place before the arc is struck.

questions.q: The permit says: "Fire watch: 60 minutes after work stops." What does this require?
o: The welders may weld for no more than 60 minutes in all
The laundry stays closed for an hour before work
The extinguisher must be ready within 60 minutes
Someone watches for fire for an hour after the welding
questions.why: Sparks can lodge in lint, cracks or fabric and smoulder before flaring up. A fire watch keeps someone checking the area, and above and below it, for the stated time after the hot work ends.

questions.q: The team makes the cut-off saw safe, tags it and reports it. How should they keep the job moving?
o: Cut the rest on the band saw while the saw is repaired
Open the motor cover themselves and look for the fault
Stop every task on the door until the saw has been mended
Keep using the saw in short bursts so that it stays cool
questions.why: A breakdown is a reason to re-plan, not to stop or to take risks. Another machine, or another order of work, keeps the job going while a competent person repairs the saw.

questions.q: The hatch will add time and cost. How should the change be handled?
o: The team adds it quietly, because the principal asked for it in person
The team refuses it, as the drawing is already approved
The supervisor agrees the cost and date with the school in writing
The team adds the hatch and sends a bill after the work
questions.why: A change is recorded and agreed before the work changes: the supervisor confirms the extra cost and time with the customer, and the drawing, cut list and plan are updated.

questions.q: At the review, the job took 26 hours against 20 planned. What is the most useful thing to record?
o: The names of the people who worked slowest
Which tasks overran and why, for future estimates
Only the final 26 hours, so the paperwork is short
That the plan was wrong and should not be used again
questions.why: A review compares actual with planned, task by task, and finds the reasons (the broken saw, the extra hatch, the mis-cut). That is how the next estimate becomes more accurate.

questions.q: Which of these targets is a SMART target?
o: Work harder on the gates this week and finish them early
Tack both gate frames to drawing G-3 by noon Friday
Make the gates as good as possible for the customer
Finish the gates soon, if there is time after other jobs
questions.why: It is specific (both frames, drawing G-3), measurable (tacked to the drawing), achievable and relevant, and time-bound (noon Friday). The others give no measure or deadline.

questions.q: A job needs a 1.2 m × 2.4 m sheet of 3 mm steel moved to the guillotine. Steel weighs about 7.85 kg per square metre for each millimetre of thickness. What should the plan say?
o: It weighs about 23 kg, so one person can carry it
It weighs about 7 kg, so it can be carried with one hand
It weighs about 680 kg, so it needs a forklift
It weighs about 68 kg, so use two people or a trolley
questions.why: 1.2 × 2.4 = 2.88 m²; 2.88 × 3 × 7.85 ≈ 68 kg. That is too heavy and awkward for one person, so the plan names two people or a sheet trolley and a safe route.
